label: Protestant Dry Democratic Nominee
detail: The party out of the presidency since 1921 is led by a Protestant who backs Prohibition, so neither religion nor liquor divides the two candidates.
assumption: The out-party nominee's Catholicism and wet stance no longer drive voters. Religious and Prohibition-based defection and turnout shift toward the 1928 baseline for a generic party candidate, and Prohibition no longer separates the parties.
facts_text: Both major parties have nominated Protestants who pledge to enforce national Prohibition.
nominee_news: He is a lifelong Protestant and has told audiences he stands firmly for keeping national Prohibition and enforcing the Eighteenth Amendment.
Dry leaders in the churches have praised him as a man who will not weaken the liquor laws.

add_planks.text: Pledges strict enforcement of the Eighteenth Amendment and the Volstead Act.

research_questions: How did Protestant Southern Democrats vote in 1928 when the nominee was not Catholic, compared with 1924?
How much of the 1928 Democratic loss in the South and Midwest was due to religion rather than Prohibition?
How did Catholic and immigrant voters in northern cities vote when the Democratic candidate was not Catholic or wet?
How did dry voters behave in elections when both major parties supported Prohibition?
source_text: The Democratic nominee in 1928 is a Protestant who supports Prohibition.
